annotations.text:
MILESTONE 1 — stages 0-3

No UI, by design. Groundwork, the Remote principal, the iroh endpoint, then events and PTY bytes. The dev probe is the only surface: two processes on one Mac, real transport, relays off.

This is the part where the design can still be wrong cheaply.

STAGE 5 — the button

Sits in the grouped sidebar header beside the terminal map and collapse controls. Hidden when the sidebar collapses comes free: the whole <aside> is unrendered.

STAGE 4 — pairing and authorization

The QR carries the Mac's NodeId and a one-time secret; scanning proves the phone was shown this screen. The Mac still asks before trusting it, because a photographed code should not be enough.
Revocation lives here. Removing a device breaks its next handshake — there is no token to expire.

STAGE 5 — two things the toggle owes you

"Anywhere" is a separate switch because it is a different consent: relays and discovery publishing turn on with it, and it says so. And a live session is never invisible — the menu-bar dot appears when a device is actually connected, not merely when the toggle is on.

STAGE 7 — first run

Scan, then wait. The phone shows the path it got (direct or relayed) and the Mac's key before anything is trusted.

STAGE 7 — seeing the terminals

Status comes from the same events the sidebar uses. The terminal is SwiftTerm over the raw PTY stream — and it never resizes the pane, or the Mac's layout would reflow to fit a phone.

STAGE 6-7 — the right pane, on a phone

Send, queue, steer, reorder, approve. These are the same turn_queue calls the desktop composer makes; the approve button sends the adapter's own keystroke. Stage 6 moves those adapter tables into Rust first, so the two clients cannot drift.
STAGE 8 is the honest gap: iOS suspends the app and the connection dies, so nothing can notify you while it is closed. Real push needs APNs and a server.
